scenes.tts: If cancer is genetic, why is it usually not inherited? Watch one pale tissue cell as a clay-colored D N A change appears. That cell divides, and the change follows its daughters. Nearby cells lack it. This is a somatic change, acquired during life, not a change carried in every cell.
scenes.caption: If cancer is genetic, why is it usually not inherited? Watch one pale tissue cell as a clay-colored DNA change appears. That cell divides, and the change follows its daughters. Nearby cells lack it. This is a somatic change, acquired during life, not a change carried in every cell.
scenes.visual: COLOR MAP FOR BOTH FILMS: pale grey = ordinary cells and DNA; clay orange = acquired somatic change; gold = inherited or germline change; blue = active growth signal or oncogene; green = working tumor-suppressor brake; red = lost function; teal = sequencing reads. Fill the frame with a six-cell tissue. A clay badge appears inside one cell. That cell divides twice while the badge copies only into its daughters. Other cells drift gently but stay pale. No molecular structures.

scenes.visual: Transform the widening clay-marked branch into the title 'One Cell, Two Routes' for two seconds. Keep the cells moving slowly behind the title.

scenes.tts: The change matters only if it changes the lineage's future. A driver lets cells divide more or die less. Its branch widens while other branches continue nearby. A passenger may ride with that branch, but it did not cause the widening. Selection acts on cells, and their D N A marks spread with them.

scenes.visual: Carry the same tissue into a large family-tree shape. The clay branch divides faster and thickens. Add one small pale passenger dot before another division; it rides through descendants without changing branch speed. Label the orange badge 'driver' only as the branch widens, and label the dot 'passenger' without changing motion.

scenes.tts: One route changes an accelerator. A proto-oncogene normally promotes growth when signals call for it. A gain-of-function change can make an oncogene overactive. Picture two gene copies, with one switch locked on. One altered allele is usually enough to change the cell's behavior. Extra gene copies or a translocation can also activate this route.

scenes.visual: Zoom into one carried cell. Replace its lineage badge with two labelled rectangular gene-copy blocks. One remains pale; one transforms into a blue slider that locks in the ON position. A division arrow begins pulsing. Keep the blue concept color fixed. Mark the picture 'schematic'.

scenes.tts: The other route changes a brake. Here are two tumor-suppressor copies. One turns red and loses function, while the other remains green. Predict: does the cell lose the brake now, or can the working copy still hold it?

scenes.visual: Transform the accelerator layout into two large brake bars inside the cell. One bar cracks and turns red. The other stays green and visibly presses against a moving division wheel, slowing it. Put the question across the top and keep the wheel straining gently.
scenes.narration: The other route changes a brake. Here are two tumor-suppressor copies. One turns red and loses function, while the other remains green. Predict: does the cell lose the brake now, or can the working copy still hold it?

scenes.visual: Hold the prediction question for thinking time. The division wheel continues a slow push against the single green brake; nothing else changes.

scenes.tts: Usually, one working copy still provides enough brake. A second loss removes that remaining function. This can give the cell a growth or survival advantage, so its branch may expand. It does not by itself guarantee cancer. Tumor-suppressor changes are therefore usually recessive within one cell. Later, the text adds exceptions to these rules.

The cell's branch begins to widen, with a small 'can expand, not must' label. Keep a small 'usually' label attached to the rule and mark the control panel 'schematic'.

scenes.tts: R B one makes the two-hit logic visible. A child may inherit one nonworking copy. Gold first-hit badges then appear in every cell, including every retinal cell. That inheritance raises risk, but it does not make every cell a tumor. Each cell still has one working copy. This germline first hit can also pass to the next generation.

scenes.visual: For one second show a small body outline with a gold 'first hit' badge in every cell, then zoom into a large cartoon retina made of pale cells. Place one gold 'first hit' badge in every retinal cell, paired with one green working-copy bar. Keep all cells the same size. Do not show a tumor yet. Label the retina and mark it 'schematic'.

scenes.tts: A rare somatic second hit removes the working copy in one retinal cell. Only that cell's descendants expand. Without an inherited first hit, both hits must arise in the same body-cell lineage. This is why inherited risk can look dominant in a family while the change remains recessive within a cell.

scenes.visual: In one retinal cell, transform the green bar into a red lost-function bar. Grow only that cell into a small expanding cluster; keep surrounding cells unchanged. Then split the frame: left begins with gold first-hit badges everywhere; right begins pale and receives two separate clay hits in one lineage. Use no route labels beyond 'inherited first hit' and 'two somatic hits'.

scenes.tts: Cancer is genetic because altered D N A passes through dividing cell lineages. It is usually not inherited because most relevant changes arise somatically. The route may activate an accelerator or remove a brake. Cell lineages expand when their D N A changes improve growth or survival. Every change a lineage carries, driver or passenger, spreads with it.
